newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy wraps up 1997 budget, calls confidence vote.
newsitem.headline: Italy wraps up 1997 budget, calls confidence vote.

text.p: Italy finally approved the last piece of its 1997 austerity budget on Thursday after a marathon parliamentary sitting and amid fresh controversy over extra finance measures the goverment plans to unveil soon.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left government won the final vote in the Chamber of Deputies (lower house) by 207 votes to 167 with one abstention.
The package of measures, designed to raise around 4.3 trillion lire ($2.6 billion), now becomes law.

But Prodi faced mounting opposition from unions and hard left allies to a forthcoming mini-budget needed after a spending overshoot derailed his hopes of qualifying for Europe's single currency on the strength of his tough 1997 package.

Prodi resorted to a confidence vote earlier this week to scrap a raft of opposition amendments to the measures approved on Thursday and had faced more filibustering after 143 deputies said they all wanted to speak ahead of the vote.
The Democratic Party of the Left, the biggest in Prodi's coalition, condemned the tactic as "infantile" and called for proceedings to go on through the night.
The chamber finally rose in the early hours and reconvened on Thursday morning for the final vote.

Shortly after it was carried, the government called a new do-or-die confidence test on an amendment it had drawn up to a decree covering reorganisation of the transport sector. The vote is expected to be held on Friday.

Because of a recent Constitutional Court ruling, the government can no longer roll over expiring decrees as had been the practice previously and has resorted to confidence votes on several occasions to turn them into law.

Prodi, who depends on support from the hard-left Communist Refoundation party for a majority in the Chamber, has won all such votes comfortably and was not expected to encounter serious difficulties in his second confidence vote of the week.
If a government loses a confidence vote it must resign.

The 1997 budget, designed to slash 62.5 trillion lire off the public sector deficit this year, will not be enough to bring Italy's deficit down to three percent of Gross Domestic Product, a requirement to join economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999.
Italy's ratio was 6.8 percent at the end of 1996.

The government has said the mini-budget, which it plans to unveil after state accounts are published next month, will contain some 14-15 trillion lire of deficit-cutting measures and will implement "structural changes".

But Communist Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti, who says no-one now seriously believes EMU will start on time as even economic powerhouse Germany struggles to get its finances in order, has ruled out support for welfare cuts or tax hikes.
He told Corriere della Sera in an interview on Thursday that if Prodi passed his mini-budget with support from a different majority to his current one, there would be a government crisis.
Sergio Cofferati, leader of Italy's biggest trades union confederation CGIL, also stepped up his opposition.
"It would be more reasonable to bring forward the 1998 budget than to pass a mini-budget," he said.
